title: Time-Series & Geospatial
tagline: BRIN indexing, downsampling, pre-aggregation, ASOF gaps, dialect mastery

placementQuiz.q: Which index is ideal for Append-Only chronological data that is rarely updated in place?
placementQuiz.explain: BRIN stores per-block summaries (min/max), tiny and fast for columnar-ordered-by-time data; updates scattered across time degrade it.

placementQuiz.q: A materialized view in time-series pipelines mainly solves:
options: Repeated expensive aggregation over the same historical window
placementQuiz.explain: Pre-aggregation turns repeated heavy GROUP BYs into point queries over stored summaries.

placementQuiz.q: ASOF JOIN semantics match two time series by:
options: Each row of A pairing with the latest row of B at or before its timestamp
Cross join with a distance cutoff
placementQuiz.explain: ASOF pairs A's row with B's most recent row whose time key is <= A's — the standard 'attach latest state' operation.

options: Aggregating 60 points into 1 summarizing row per hour
placementQuiz.explain: Downsampling reduces resolution by grouping and summarizing (avg/sum/min/max), shrinking storage and speeding scans without losing trend.

placementQuiz.q: For a 12-month retention window on append-only logs, which storage path helps the most?
placementQuiz.explain: Time partitioning prunes whole chunks for retention deletion and range queries; the dominant win in production time-series stores.

blocks.md: **Beginner SQL optimizes query text; advanced SQL optimizes storage layout. Time-series is a storage problem first, a query problem second.**

Append-only chronological data has a special shape: rows are written in near-time order and rarely updated. That single fact changes everything — BRIN beats B-tree for scans, partitions beat a single giant heap, and precomputed aggregates beat recomputation. Learn to think: *what does the storage already know about the time order?*

items: Time-ordered writes => block-level summaries make sense (BRIN)
Retention windows => partition pruning beats DELETE + VACUUM
Repeated analytics => materialize the heavy aggregation
Point lookups ('latest per id') => a different beast: b-tree / DISTINCT ON

blocks.text: Why B-tree is often the wrong default

blocks.md: A B-tree on ts gives fast point and range lookups but its leaf pages grow with every insert, and on a 10B-row table the tree is deep and cache-hostile. BRIN instead records, per 128-page block range, the min and max ts. For a range query the planner skips whole ranges with no match — reading only the ranges that intersect your window.

-- BRIN shines on >1B rows, append-heavy, time-ordered
-- Brin: pages_per_range trades index size vs scan selectivity
blocks.mysql: -- MySQL: no BRIN. Clustered PK on time + partition pruning mimics it

blocks.title: EXPLAIN — BRIN range scan on 1B rows

blocks.md: **BRIN degrades if rows are inserted out of time order** (backfilled history, imports, reindex). Reordering or partitioning per time chunk keeps block summaries honest.

items.q: BRIN indexes are most effective when:
options: Rows are randomly distributed by key
Rows arrive roughly time-ordered and are rarely updated
The lookup key is a UUID
items.explain: Block-range min/max summaries only help when similar keys cluster in the same blocks — true for append-ordered time data.

items.q: A BRIN scan skips a block range when:
options: The range's recorded min/max does not overlap the WHERE window
The range has no index entries
items.explain: Pruning is exactly that: the planner checks each range's min/max against the predicate and discards non-overlapping ranges.

blocks.label: hourly rollup materialized view
blocks.code:
-- Materialized hourly rollup (12 months retention)
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW hourly_metric AS
SELECT date_trunc('hour', ts) AS hour_bucket,
       entity_id,
       COUNT(*)    AS n,
       SUM(value)  AS sum,
       MIN(value)  AS min,
       MAX(value)  AS max,
       AVG(value)  AS avg
FROM raw_metric
WHERE ts > now() - INTERVAL '12 months'
GROUP BY 1, 2;

-- Refresh per hour (incremental vs full rewrite — see note)
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY hourly_metric;
blocks.pg:
-- REFRESH CONCURRENTLY needs a unique index on the matview
-- TimescaleDB: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... WITH (timescaledb.continuous)
blocks.mysql:
-- MySQL: no materialized views; schedule INSERT ... SELECT
-- into a rollup table, or use a scheduled event

blocks.label: two-stage filter
blocks.code:
-- 1) Coarse window filter on a tiny index/column
-- 2) Precise predicate only inside the window
SELECT date_trunc('day', ts) AS day_bucket, AVG(value)
FROM events
WHERE ts >= now() - INTERVAL '90 days'
  AND ts <  now()             -- coarse
  AND value IS NOT NULL       -- precise
GROUP BY day_bucket;
blocks.pg: -- planner orders filters by cost; make coarse cheap
blocks.mysql: -- same principle: push the partitioning predicate first

blocks.md: Rule of thumb: **materialize the summary the analyst asks for every week, not the one they ask for once.** Rollups pay for themselves on the 2nd repeated query.

items.q: A rollup view storing COUNT/SUM/MIN/MAX per hour:
options: Can answer AVG per day via SUM/COUNT aggregates
items.explain: SUM(SUM) / SUM(COUNT) reconstructs a weighted average — keeping sufficient statistics enables higher-level rollups.

items.q: Refreshing a time-series materialized view concurrently requires:
options: A primary key on the base table
A unique index on the materialized view
The view to be a view, not a table
items.explain: Concurrent refresh tracks changed rows via a unique index on the matview so readers aren't blocked during the refresh.

blocks.text: ASOF: attach the latest known state

blocks.label: ASOF join via DISTINCT ON
blocks.code:
-- For each price tick, attach the latest rate at or before it
WITH prices AS (
  SELECT ts, price FROM trades
), rates AS (
  SELECT ts AS rate_ts, rate FROM fx_rates
)
SELECT DISTINCT ON (p.ts)
  p.ts, p.price,
  r.rate
FROM prices p
LEFT JOIN rates r ON r.rate_ts <= p.ts
ORDER BY p.ts, r.rate_ts DESC;
blocks.pg:
-- DISTINCT ON picks the closest preceding rate row
-- PostgreSQL's classic ASOF; kysoh/join-expansion for big data
blocks.mysql:
-- MySQL: correlated scalar subquery
SELECT p.ts, p.price,
  (SELECT r.rate FROM fx_rates r
   WHERE r.rate_ts <= p.ts ORDER BY r.rate_ts DESC LIMIT 1) AS rate
FROM trades p;
blocks.py-pandas:
# pandas merge_asof
import pandas as pd
merge_asof(prices.sort_values('ts'), rates.sort_values('ts'),
           on='ts', direction='backward')

blocks.label: linear interpolation
blocks.code:
-- Linear interpolation between surrounding observations
-- (weighted split of the interval by time distance)
WITH filled AS (
  SELECT
    ts,
    value,
    LAG(value IGNORE NULLS)  OVER (ORDER BY ts) AS prev_val,
    LAG(ts     IGNORE NULLS)  OVER (ORDER BY ts) AS prev_ts,
    LEAD(value IGNORE NULLS) OVER (ORDER BY ts) AS next_val,
    LEAD(ts     IGNORE NULLS) OVER (ORDER BY ts) AS next_ts
  FROM measurements
)
SELECT
  ts,
  value,
  COALESCE(value,
    prev_val + (next_val - prev_val) *
      (EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (ts - prev_ts)) /
       EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (next_ts - prev_ts)))
  ) AS interp
FROM filled;
blocks.pg: -- IGNORE NULLS lets LAG skip NULLs (PG 10+)
blocks.mysql: -- MySQL: fill via correlated subqueries to next/prev non-null

blocks.md: Interpolation assumes continuity; ASOF assumes 'latest state applies'. **Pick by domain.** Financial rates are usually ASOF; temperature is usually linear. Encoding the wrong assumption invalidates the model downstream.

items.q: merge_asof(direction='backward') is the pandas sibling of:
items.explain: Both pair each A-row with the most recent B-row whose key is <=; pandas names it direction='backward'.

items.q: DISTINCT ON (p.ts) ... ORDER BY p.ts, r.rate_ts DESC picks:
options: The latest rate row at or before p.ts
items.explain: DISTINCT ON keeps the first row per p.ts after ORDER BY sorts rates newest-first within the on-or-before set.

items.explain: The <-> operator is a PostGIS/PostgreSQL native — other engines need explicit distance-sorted plans.

revisionCard: BRIN (block-range min/max) beats B-tree for scans on append-ordered time data; breaks on out-of-order inserts.
Storage layout decides query speed: partition by time, index per partition, keep columns narrow.
Rollups: materialize hourly from raw, monthly from hourly; carry COUNT/SUM/MIN/MAX so higher levels stay derivable.
ASOF = attach latest on-or-before state; DISTINCT ON in pg, correlated subquery in MySQL, merge_asof in pandas.
Interpolation vs ASOF is a domain decision — continuity vs 'latest state applies'.
Dialect gaps: date_trunc (pg) vs DATE_FORMAT (mysql) vs resample (pandas); KNN <-> is pg-only.

glossary.def: Block Range INdex storing per-range min/max; compact scans for naturally time-sorted data.
BRIN tuning knob = blocks summarized per index entry; higher = smaller index, coarser pruning.
Joins each A-row to the latest B-row with key <= A's, attaching the 'current state'.
Precomputed aggregate table reducing raw volume into summaries at coarser granularity.
Planner dropping irrelevant partitions from a range-partitioned table based on WHERE quals.
pandas function implementing backward/forward ASOF semantics with log10 tolerance.
